note: Delivery §5a.3 — the canonical, domain-separated registration proof. The signature input is the JCS serialization (RFC 8785) of the object with "sig" omitted; the signature is Ed25519 under "principal". The "v" constant is inside the signed bytes and is the domain tag.
domainTagNote: rltp-carrier-proof/0.1 appears in no other signed artifact of this stack. A verifier MUST reject an object whose v is not byte-equal to this constant.
challengeEncoding: exactly 32 raw bytes, canonical unpadded base64url — exactly 43 characters
sigEncoding: Ed25519 over the JCS bytes, carried as canonical base58btc with the z multibase prefix — the same signature encoding and canonicity rule Encounter 2.3 imposes on every signature of this stack

keys.principalSeedNote: the Ed25519 seed of the control principal of identity-derivation.json carrierRelationship case 1 (did:web:carrier.example)
keys.rkidNote: documented sample X25519 keys, sha2-256 of the ASCII labels rltp/vector/carrier-proof/rkid-1 and -2

generationMonotonicity.note: Delivery §5a.3 — a rebind binds only on a STRICTLY HIGHER generation than the one the carrier last accepted. Equal generation with the same principal is registered(idempotent); equal generation with a different principal is refused (the carrier cannot decide a tie the register decides by nonce bytes); lower is refused(stale-generation). This is what stops a device restored from an older backup — which still holds root IKM, the older nonce and the rkid private key, and can therefore prove everything — from rolling the binding back.

cases.case: a restored device presents generation 1 with valid proofs
the same generation, the same principal
the same generation, a DIFFERENT principal — a tie the carrier cannot decide

equalGenerationTie.note: Delivery §5a.3 / Identity §7a.3 — the composite the two state machines did not cover separately. The register decides an equal-generation race by the smallest nonce bytes; the carrier cannot see them and MUST NOT be given a value that reconstructs their order (any such value is order-preserving in the nonce, hence identical at every carrier of that relationship — a cross-carrier join key, Identity §7a.4). So refused(stale-generation) at an equal generation is a WAIT STATE, and the healing path is a rotation. A rotation draws a FRESH random nonce (Identity §7a.3) and the principal depends on (C, N) and not on the generation (§7a.4) — so the healing step derives a NEW principal, and this vector carries that derivation rather than reusing a value.

steps.step: the device holding the LARGER nonce reaches the carrier first and binds
the registers merge: the SMALLER nonce is canonical (Identity §7a.3) — the carrier learns nothing of this
the canonical device presents its rebind: equal generation, different principal
it rotates — a FRESH nonce at generation + 1, so the principal is newly derived and differs from both tie candidates

equalGenerationTie.healingCost: exactly one rotation, borne by the honest case that produced the tie
equalGenerationTie.rotationNonceNote: documented sample, deterministic for this vector set (sha2-256 of the ASCII label "rltp/vector/carrier-relationship/nonce-3")

tieAtTheMaximum.note: Delivery §5a.3 / Identity §7a.3 — the doubly theoretical corner: a tie AT the generation maximum, where no rotation is available. The exit is not re-addressing (a holder cannot elect that) but the rule that was already there: entries are superseded, NEVER DELETED, so every device retains the bound entry and can derive its principal. The binding stands and stays collectable; what is lost is only the ability to change which of two principals holds it.
tieAtTheMaximum.why: collection and conclusion require possession of the BOUND principal's key; every device derives it from the retained superseded entry, so deposits arrive, are collected and are concluded
remainingLevers: Identity §7a.2's move to a different configured C (different principals, N untouched)
a genuinely new relationship chain — a social event of the companions, never an instruction

releasedAndReRegistered.note: Delivery §5a.3/§5a.9 — after the two-phase wind-up releases queue and binding, a device from an old backup still holds the older nonce and the rkid private key and can prove everything. The binding tombstone (rkid, highest generation ever accepted) is what keeps 'possession of a superseded generation is possession of nothing' true past the release.

steps.step: the binding is released at the end of the wind-up
a restored device presents generation 1 with valid proofs
the same device presents generation 2 — equal, not greater
the holder registers afresh at generation 3

releasedAndReRegistered.residual: The tombstone does not expire in time; it is released only by the capacity rule of Delivery §4.4 — at max-binding-tombstones the OLDEST by release time is evicted. For an evicted rkid the anti-resurrection guarantee ends, and that consequence is reachable only by a party holding BOTH halves (the principal's Ed25519 key, derivable only from the root IKM and that nonce, and the rkid's X25519 private key) — that is the person or a device holding their state, never a third party. Forcing eviction costs the attacker a full registration plus an orphan-horizon of waiting per tombstone, so it is metered and slow.

evictionRule.evicts: the oldest tombstone by release time
evictionRule.consequenceForEvictedRkid: the anti-resurrection guarantee ends for that address
evictionRule.reachableBy: only a party holding both the principal key and the rkid private key
evictionRule.attackerCostPerTombstone: one full registration (both proofs, one challenge charge, registration capacity) plus one orphan-horizon of waiting

collection.note: purpose=collect: rkid and addressChallenge are ABSENT — those acts are authorized per session, not per address. Their absence is part of the JCS bytes.

negatives.note: Each negative changes one value; the JCS bytes therefore differ from the registration bytes and the shipped signature MUST NOT verify over them. This is the executable form of "the proof is not transplantable".

cases.case: purpose changed from register to rebind

rateStateMachine.note: Delivery §4.4 `rate` — a token bucket counted in integer MICRO-tokens, so no rounding remainder can be lost. State is one integer `micro`; a millisecond is worth exactly `admission-rate-max` micro-tokens; one deposit costs `windowMs`. The verdict reads only state; a refusal changes nothing.
rateStateMachine.configurationNote: window=1000 ms and max=3 is deliberately NOT evenly divisible — the previous vector used PT1M/3 and could not have caught the whole-token rounding fault (round-4 B-4).
rateStateMachine.refill: micro := min(max*windowMs, micro + elapsedMs*max); an admitted deposit subtracts windowMs; a refusal subtracts nothing
rateStateMachine.restartRule: only `micro` is persisted; on restart lastRefill := the first observed monotonic instant and NO elapsed credit crosses the restart. A carrier that cannot recover `micro` starts the queue empty (micro = 0).
rateStateMachine.counterExampleNote: The whole-token casting granted one token at 334 ms and refused at 667 ms, while two requests arriving together at 667 ms both succeeded. In micro-tokens both sequences admit exactly two deposits after the bucket is empty: capacity is a function of elapsed time alone.

polledAt334And667.step: empty the fresh bucket (three deposits, no time)
third — the bucket is now empty
the round-4 case: a request at 334 ms
and a second at 667 ms — under whole tokens this was refused
a refusal changes nothing (no time passed)

bothAt667.step: both requests arrive only at 667 ms: first

acrossRestart.step: process restarts here — only micro persists, no elapsed credit crosses
first request after restart, at the first observed instant

challengeChargeMachine.note: Delivery §4.4 — a challenge slot is a CHARGE, not a lock. It is taken at the budget check (step (b) of the ordering), before any randomness, sealing or asymmetric operation, and lapses only on challenge-lifetime — never by completion, abandonment, a closed connection, or a restart.
challengeChargeMachine.restartRule: On restart the full budget counts as held with a single deadline of restart + challenge-lifetime; no per-request state is persisted, and the carrier resumes with strictly less capacity than it had.

serialCompletions.step: issue 1 (charge taken at the budget check, before any key operation)
complete it immediately — the exchange ends, the charge does not
a fourth request, though every earlier exchange COMPLETED
and a fifth — completion never refunds
after most of the lifetime, still full
once the first charge lapses, one slot returns

acrossRestart.step: carrier restarts here — full budget held, deadline = restart + challenge-lifetime
a request right after the restart
and one just before the deadline
after the deadline the budget is free again

reserveAndStarvation.note: Delivery §4.4/§5a.5 — the reserve is PER BOUND ADDRESS, not a pool: every bound rkid has its own single reserved charge, reachable only by naming that rkid. Unknown-rkid requests share the unreserved pool (max-open-challenges). Repeated starvation of the UNRESERVED pool is real and remains a named residual; it cannot reach any bound address's reserved charge.

declaration.reserve: one per bound rkid, not drawn from max-open-challenges

sequence.step: attacker fills the unreserved pool with unknown rkids
and again — the unreserved pool is full
a further unknown rkid is refused: the pool is the residual
rkid-A's own reserved charge is untouched by all of that
rkid-B's too — reserves do not compete with each other
a second request for rkid-A while its charge is live
the counterpart of rkid-A holds A's charge — and reaches no other address
after the lapse the attacker re-takes the unreserved pool: NOT self-healing
and rkid-B is still free to return

duplicateRule.note: Delivery §5a.5 — two submissions to one queue are duplicates IFF their sealed envelopes are byte-identical (rkid, epk, nonce, ciphertext). A key-blind carrier can compare nothing else. Re-sealing one document yields a fresh epk/nonce/ciphertext and is therefore NOT a duplicate at the carrier; §6.2 absorbs that at the receiver, after decryption, on the document digest.
duplicateRule.metering: A duplicate consumes the admission resource exactly like an admitted submission and consumes NO storage; the check sits after the resource charge and before storage admission, so it can neither bypass the charge nor reach the store.
duplicateRule.retention: The comparison value is held exactly as long as the deposit is held; after conclusion or give-up a byte-identical re-presentation is a NEW submission and is admitted.

cases.case: byte-identical replay of an admitted envelope
the SAME document re-sealed — fresh epk, nonce and ciphertext
identical bytes but a different rkid — a different queue entirely
byte-identical re-presentation AFTER the first deposit was concluded

queueFloorAccounting.note: Delivery §4.4 — committed = sum over LIVE queues of max(used, queue-floor) + sum over CLOSING queues of used, evaluated on the occupancy AFTER admission. A queue below its floor can always grow to its floor, because that admission does not move committed at all.

cases.case: the round-11 counter-example: A at its floor, B one byte below, a 1-byte deposit to B
cases.why: B stays within its floor, so max(used,floor) does not change — the floor guarantee is arithmetic, not a promise

cases.case: the same queue one byte above its floor
cases.why: above the floor every byte raises committed, and the bound is reached

cases.case: a closing queue holds bytes: it contributes used, not a floor
cases.why: closing bytes stay visible in committed and cannot be handed out twice; the closing queue needs no floor, having nothing left to guarantee
